text: An engineer accidentally runs UPDATE on a large table, corrupting millions of rows. They need to restore the table to 5 minutes ago. What is the fastest method?

options.A: Restore from Fail-safe via Snowflake Support
options.B: CREATE OR REPLACE TABLE t1 AS SELECT * FROM t1 AT(OFFSET => -300) — restores from Time Travel
options.C: UNDROP TABLE t1
options.D: Restore from an external backup system

explanation: CTAS from Time Travel (AT OFFSET => -300 = 5 minutes ago) is the fastest self-service recovery for data corruption. UNDROP is for dropped tables. Fail-safe requires Support and takes time. This is faster than any external backup.

text: A database clone is created. The original table within it is then updated with 1 million new rows. Does the clone's storage increase?

options.A: Yes — the clone mirrors all changes to the original
options.B: No — the clone's data remains at the point-in-time of cloning. Only the ORIGINAL's storage increases (for new micro-partitions).
options.C: Both increase equally
options.D: Neither increases until the clone is queried

explanation: Clones are independent after creation. Changes to the original create new micro-partitions that are NOT shared with the clone. The clone retains its snapshot. Only diverged data costs additional storage.

text: Can you create a clone of a table that is inside a shared database (consumer side)?

options.A: Yes — consumers can clone any shared object
options.B: No — consumers do not have OWNERSHIP on shared objects, which is required for cloning
options.C: Yes, but only with ACCOUNTADMIN
options.D: Yes, but the clone is read-only

explanation: Cloning requires OWNERSHIP on the source object. Consumers have IMPORTED PRIVILEGES (read-only) on shared data, not OWNERSHIP. To copy data, use CREATE TABLE AS SELECT instead.

text: Replication lag between primary and secondary databases is 2 hours. A query on the secondary returns data that is 2 hours stale. Is this expected?

options.A: No — secondaries should always be real-time
options.B: Yes — replication lag determines how fresh the secondary is. The secondary reflects the state from the last successful refresh.
options.C: No — if lag exceeds 1 hour, an error is raised

explanation: Secondary databases are only as current as the last successful replication refresh. Between refreshes, data is stale by the lag duration. This is expected behavior for async replication.

text: An engineer sets DATA_RETENTION_TIME_IN_DAYS = 0 on a table. What is the practical effect?

options.A: Time Travel is completely disabled — no AT/BEFORE queries, no UNDROP for that table
options.B: Time Travel is set to the account default
options.C: Only UNDROP is disabled; AT queries still work

explanation: Setting retention to 0 disables Time Travel entirely for that object. No historical queries (AT/BEFORE), no UNDROP capability. Dropped data goes directly to Fail-safe (for permanent tables) or is lost (for transient).

text: A provider runs SHOW SHARES and sees a share with 3 consumer accounts listed. One consumer has not yet created a database from the share. Does that consumer incur any cost to the provider?

options.A: Yes — storage is duplicated for each consumer
options.B: No — until a consumer creates the database, there is no cost. And even after, direct shares are zero-copy (no storage duplication).
options.C: Yes — compute charges begin at share creation
options.D: Only if the consumer is a Reader Account

explanation: Direct shares are zero-copy — no data is duplicated for consumers. Consumers query the provider's data in place. No cost to the provider for regular consumers (consumers use their own warehouse). Only Reader Accounts cost the provider compute.

text: A share contains a secure view that references TWO tables from the SAME database. Does the provider need REFERENCE_USAGE grants?

options.A: Yes — REFERENCE_USAGE is always required for views in shares
options.B: No — REFERENCE_USAGE is only needed when referencing objects from a DIFFERENT database than the shared database
options.C: Only if one table is in a different schema

explanation: REFERENCE_USAGE is required only for cross-database references. If the secure view and all its referenced tables are in the same database (the one being shared), standard USAGE/SELECT grants suffice.

text: A provider shares a table. The consumer runs SELECT COUNT(*) and gets 1 million rows. The provider then deletes 500K rows. What does the consumer see next query?

options.A: Still 1 million (cached copy)
options.B: 500K — shared data reflects real-time changes from the provider immediately
options.C: 1 million until the consumer refreshes
options.D: An error because the data changed

explanation: Shared data is live (zero-copy, real-time access to provider's data). When the provider deletes rows, the consumer immediately sees the updated state on their next query. No refresh needed.

text: A Marketplace listing is set to 'Free'. Does the consumer incur any cost at all?

options.A: No costs whatsoever
options.B: No listing fee, but the consumer still pays for their own WAREHOUSE COMPUTE when querying the shared data
options.C: Only storage costs

explanation: 'Free' means no charge from the provider for the data. But the consumer uses their own warehouse to query it, so they pay their normal compute credits. Storage is zero-copy (no consumer storage cost for direct shares).

text: A provider publishes a listing on the Marketplace. Can they see which specific queries consumers run against the shared data?

options.A: Yes — full query text is visible to providers
options.B: No — providers can see usage metrics (query count, bytes scanned) but NOT the actual query text consumers execute
options.C: Only with Business Critical Edition

explanation: Providers get aggregated usage telemetry (LISTING_TELEMETRY_DAILY, MONETIZED_USAGE_DAILY) but cannot see individual consumer query text. This protects consumer privacy while giving providers usage insights.

text: A table has 30-day Time Travel. An engineer queries it with AT(TIMESTAMP => '2025-05-01 00:00:00'::TIMESTAMP). Today is May 28, 2026. What happens?

options.A: Data from May 1 2025 is returned
options.B: An error — the requested time is beyond the 30-day Time Travel retention window
options.C: Current data is returned as a fallback

explanation: Time Travel only covers the configured retention period. 30 days of retention from today (May 28 2026) goes back to April 28 2026. May 1 2025 is over a year ago — well beyond retention. An error is returned.

text: A consumer queries a shared secure view that includes CURRENT_ROLE() in the SELECT list. What value do they see?

options.A: The provider's role
options.B: The consumer's currently active role — context functions execute in the consumer's session
options.C: NULL — context functions are blocked in shares

explanation: Context functions (CURRENT_ROLE, CURRENT_USER, CURRENT_ACCOUNT) execute in the consumer's session context. The secure view definition uses them for dynamic filtering, returning values relevant to the consumer.

text: Which TWO actions can a consumer perform on shared data? (Select TWO)

options.A: SELECT (read) the data
options.B: INSERT new rows into shared tables
options.C: Create views on top of shared objects

explanation: Consumers can: SELECT shared data, create their own views/streams on top of it, and join with their local tables. They CANNOT: INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, DROP, ALTER, or CLONE shared objects.

text: A schema with MANAGED ACCESS is cloned. Does the clone retain the managed access property?

options.A: No — clones always use standard access
options.B: Yes — the MANAGED ACCESS property is cloned along with the schema
options.C: Only if explicitly specified in the CLONE command

explanation: Cloning preserves the schema's properties, including WITH MANAGED ACCESS. The cloned schema retains centralized grant control where only the schema owner (or MANAGE GRANTS holders) can grant access.

text: A provider offers a listing in the Marketplace. A consumer in a different cloud (provider on AWS, consumer on Azure) gets the listing via Auto-Fulfillment. Where does the consumer query data from?

options.A: The provider's AWS region directly via cross-cloud networking
options.B: A replicated copy in the consumer's Azure region — Auto-Fulfillment replicates data to the consumer's region
options.C: A shared S3 bucket accessible from Azure
options.D: The consumer must switch to an AWS account

explanation: Auto-Fulfillment replicates data to the consumer's region/cloud. The consumer queries from a local copy in their Azure region. This avoids cross-cloud network latency but costs the provider storage/compute for replication.

text: What happens when a database containing a table with 90-day retention is dropped? The database has 1-day retention.

options.A: The table retains its 90-day window independently
options.B: UNDROP DATABASE has only 1 day — after that, both the database AND its tables are gone regardless of individual table retention
options.C: The table's 90-day retention overrides
options.D: Both retention values are added (91 days)

explanation: When a container is dropped, the container's retention governs UNDROP timing. After 1 day, the database (and everything inside) leaves Time Travel. Individual object retention is irrelevant when the parent container is dropped.

text: Can a consumer join shared data with their own local tables?

options.A: No — shared data can only be queried in isolation
options.B: Yes — consumers can JOIN shared tables with their own tables, create views combining both, and run any read operations
options.C: Only with ACCOUNTADMIN role

explanation: Consumers can freely JOIN shared data with their local tables, create views that combine shared and local data, and perform any read-only operations. This is a key value proposition of Snowflake sharing.

text: CREATE DATA EXCHANGE LISTING privilege is required for which action?

options.A: Consuming a Marketplace listing
options.B: Creating and publishing a listing as a provider on a Data Exchange
options.C: Creating a Reader Account

explanation: CREATE DATA EXCHANGE LISTING is the privilege for providers to create and publish listings. Consumers need IMPORT SHARE to get/install listings. Different privileges for different sides of the sharing relationship.

text: Two tables are cloned at the same time from the same source. Do the two clones share micro-partitions with each other?

options.A: No — each clone is independent
options.B: Yes — both clones AND the source all share the same underlying micro-partitions until any of them diverges
options.C: Only if created in the same transaction
options.D: Only the first clone shares with the source

explanation: Zero-copy cloning means all copies (source + all clones) reference the same underlying micro-partitions. When any copy diverges (DML), only the changed partitions are new. All unchanged data remains shared.

text: A provider removes a table from a share (REVOKE SELECT ... FROM SHARE). The consumer had been querying it. What happens to their existing queries/views that reference it?

options.A: They continue working with cached data
options.B: They immediately fail — the object is no longer accessible. Consumer views referencing it will error on next query.
options.C: They work for 24 more hours
options.D: The consumer is notified but access continues

explanation: When a provider revokes an object from a share, it becomes immediately inaccessible to consumers. Any consumer views, streams, or queries referencing that object will fail immediately on the next execution.
